title: Sephardi and Mizrahi practice
hook: often less divided into movements, with traditional practice across a wide range

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: religious zionism. An Orthodox stream that reads the State of Israel as the first flowering of redemption. Did you try stating a view in its holders' own words? Today closes the week with a different kind of map. Day one thousand two hundred eighteen.

A tall case of carved silver stands on the reader's table. Someone unlatches it and swings it open like a cabinet, and there is the Torah scroll, upright, facing the room. It will be read standing, never laid flat. The case is called a tik. In the rows facing it on this Shabbat morning sits a man who keeps every detail of the day and walked here, and next to him his nephew, who drove, parked around the corner, and is singing louder than anyone. They pray from the same book, to the tunes their families brought from far away. Nobody checks a label at the door. Today, a way of being Jewish that this week's map of movements doesn't quite fit.
screen: `A SCROLL STANDING IN ITS CASE.` → `ONE WALKED, ONE DROVE.` → `NO LABEL AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Sephardi and Mizrahi practice. Turn it four ways. First, the names. Obadiah speaks of "the captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Sepharad." Tradition came to read Sepharad as Spain, and Sephardi Jews trace their families to Spain and Portugal, and from there to North Africa, the Ottoman lands and beyond. Mizrahi comes from mizrach, east: the psalm's "as far as the east is from the west" uses that word. Mizrahi Jews come from lands like Iraq, Iran, Yemen and Syria. The two words overlap, and families use them differently. Second, the law. Rabbi Joseph Karo wrote the Shulchan Aruch largely following Sephardi practice. Rabbi Moses Isserles added notes for Ashkenazi Jews, and those notes are printed on the same page. One code, two customs, side by side. Third, the movements. The split into Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and others grew up among Ashkenazi Jews in Europe and America. Often, in Sephardi and Mizrahi communities, the synagogue stayed traditional, and people across a wide range of personal observance kept coming, without anyone needing a new label for themselves. Fourth, the custom. The tik is one. In some synagogues it is carved wood, in others silver, and the scroll inside is read standing, like a book set on its spine. Small things like that, melodies, foods, the order of prayers, carry a home across centuries and borders. That's today's line. This week walked from what all the streams share, through what they debate, to Orthodoxy and its streams, and ends here, where tradition is less a position than a house.
screen: `SEPHARAD AND THE EAST.` · `ONE CODE, TWO CUSTOMS.` · `LESS DIVIDED INTO MOVEMENTS.` · `THE TORAH STANDING IN ITS CASE.` · then, large: `TRADITION AS HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one Sephardi custom, the tik. Settle, and breathe. Picture the scroll standing upright in its case, the doors of the case opening like a cabinet, the reader leaning in to the words without ever laying the scroll down. Now bring to mind one custom from your own family, a dish, a song, a way of setting the table, that came from somewhere far away. Hold the two side by side, the case and your custom. Notice how a small thing carries a whole place. Then let both rest. The bell holds the time.

Sephardi and Mizrahi practice. Jewish life from Spain, North Africa and the lands to the east: often less divided into movements, with traditional synagogues that welcome a wide range of observance. Today's word.

Your line: tradition as home. Today, keep one small custom from your own family on purpose, and notice what it carries. Seven days, from what they share to tradition as home. Day one thousand two hundred eighteen.
